scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that caution toward new leaders is wise while arguing 'always' is too strict; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: A new leader arrives with promises but no proven record of keeping them.
Some people claim that it is always appropriate to remain skeptical of new leaders until they show they are worthy of trust.
I agree that healthy caution is wise, but I believe the word always makes the claim too strict.
First, a reasonable skepticism toward new leaders is usually wise.
New leaders often make grand promises that they may not be able to keep.
For example, a new manager who vows great change should be judged by results, not words.
This shows that careful judgment protects people from being misled by empty promises.
History is full of leaders who won trust too easily and then abused it.
A little caution gives a new leader the chance to prove herself by her actions.
To this extent, skepticism toward new leaders is sensible.
Second, however, remaining skeptical in every case would be harmful.
Some level of trust is needed for any leader to do her job at all.
Consider a team that refuses to cooperate with a capable new leader out of constant suspicion.
Such distrust can paralyse an organisation and prevent any progress.
Endless skepticism can also be unfair to leaders who have done nothing to deserve it.
Sometimes a leader's clear record or character earns reasonable trust from the start.
Skepticism, then, should be healthy rather than absolute and unending.
In conclusion, a reasonable caution toward new leaders is usually wise.
But remaining skeptical in every case would block cooperation and progress.
The wisest approach watches new leaders carefully while still giving them a fair chance to earn trust.
